question_reviews.independent_solution: D=R\{0}. f=0 implies x^2+1=0, so there are no real x-intercepts and no y-intercept. f'=1-1/x^2=(x^2-1)/x^2 is positive for |x|>1 and negative for 0<|x|<1, giving local maximum (-1,-2) and local minimum (1,2). For x>0, f-2=(x-1)^2/x>=0; for x<0, f+2=(x+1)^2/x<=0. Together with the infinite end limits this gives branch ranges (-infinity,-2] and [2,infinity), and not R. f tends to -infinity at 0- and +infinity at 0+, so x=0 is vertical; f-x=1/x tends to 0 at both infinite ends, so y=x is oblique. The complete true set is {a,b,c,e}.

question_reviews.independent_solution: D=R\{0}. h=(x^3+2)/x has exactly one x-intercept at -cuberoot(2) and none on the y-axis. As x approaches 0-, 2/x dominates and h tends to -infinity; at 0+ it tends to +infinity. At either infinite end h-x^2=2/x tends to 0. h'=2x-2/x^2=2(x^3-1)/x^2 is negative for every negative x, negative on (0,1), and positive on (1,infinity). The negative branch decreases continuously from +infinity to -infinity and covers R. The positive branch has minimum h(1)=3; independently h-3=(x-1)^2(x+2)/x>=0 for x>0, and both positive-branch ends tend to +infinity. Its range is [3,infinity), but the full range is R. The point (-1,-1) has derivative -4 and is not an extremum. The complete true set is {b,c,e,g}.

option_checks.evidence: The left limit is -infinity, not +infinity, because x^2 tends to 0 while 2/x tends to -infinity as x approaches 0-. Only the right limit is +infinity.
The denominator excludes exactly x=0. For nonzero x, h=0 is equivalent to x^3+2=0, whose unique real root is -cuberoot(2). The excluded point 0 rules out a y-intercept.

The two divergent one-sided limits give vertical asymptote x=0. The exact identity h-x^2=2/x tends to 0 at both +infinity and -infinity. This statement asserts quadratic asymptotic behavior, not a straight oblique line.

The minimum 3 holds only on the positive branch. On the full domain h(-1)=-1<3 and h tends to -infinity at 0-, so no full-domain minimum exists. The negative branch alone covers R, making the proposed full range [3,infinity) false.

For x<0, x^3-1<0 and x^2>0, so h'<0 everywhere. The limits are +infinity at -infinity and -infinity at 0-. Continuity and strict decrease on that component yield every real y-value; hence the full range is R.
h' is negative throughout (-infinity,0), including (-1,0); no increasing interval or negative-side turning point occurs. Although h(-1)=-1, h'(-1)=-4, so (-1,-1) is not a local minimum.

For positive x, h'<0 on (0,1), h'>0 on (1,infinity), and h(1)=3. Also h-3=(x-1)^2(x+2)/x>=0 on x>0, with equality only at 1. Both positive-branch ends tend to +infinity, so that branch has range [3,infinity).
